383	\section{Log-Probability Score Compression}\label{app:logprob_ties}
384	
385	Under constrained decoding, log-probability scores are severely compressed within instances, limiting per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}).
386	The median within-instance LP range is only 0.041, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$).
387	At $\varepsilon{=}0.05$, 60.3\% of instances have a within-sample range below the threshold, leaving LP unable to meaningfully distinguish candidates.
388	For comparison, SJ has only 12.5\% tied instances at the same threshold---SJ's advantage over LP for selection is one of score resolution, not information content.
389	
390	\begin{table}[t]
391	\centering
392	\small
393	\caption{Log-probability score compression on SciERC NER ($N{=}8$, $n{=}529$). ``Tied'' = fraction of instances where within-instance LP range ${<}\varepsilon$.}
394	\label{tab:logprob_ties}
395	\begin{tabular}{lc}
396	\toprule
397	$\varepsilon$ threshold & Tied instances (\%) \\
398	\midrule
399	0.01 & 1.1\% \\
400	0.05 & 60.3\% \\
401	0.1  & ${\sim}$84\% \\
402	0.5  & ${\sim}$99\% \\
403	\bottomrule
404	\end{tabular}
405	\end{table}
406	
407	\paragraph{Non-tied subset.}
408	Among instances with LP range ${\geq}0.05$ ($n{=}210$, 40\% of total), log-probability selection \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp F1, $p{=}0.01$), and within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ rises from 0.08 (tied subset) to 0.39 (non-tied subset).
409	This confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information but is resolution-limited---the signal exists but is compressed below the discrimination threshold for most instances.
410	A free-form decoding ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}) confirms this compression is intrinsic, not decoding-regime-specific.
411	
412	\section{RE Conditional Selection}\label{app:re_conditional_selection}
```

9	\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}
10	\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.
11	Consensus-proximity selection (\S\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
12	\textit{Layer 2 (score compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 13--18~pp oracle headroom.
13	LP scores are severely compressed: 60\% of instances have a within-sample range below 0.05, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$; Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}).
14	In the 40\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\rho$: 0.08$\to$0.39).
15	This diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression is the primary mechanistic bottleneck.
16	A controlled ablation (\S\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that this compression is intrinsic to the model and task, not an artifact of constrained decoding.
17	Diversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.

    "originalFile": "\\section{Discussion}\\label{sec:discussion}\n\n\\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}\nFor per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\\rho{=}0.38$), though EM leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).\nSignal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.\nAt higher sample sizes ($N{=}16$), SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\\Delta{=}0.002$) with lower cross-seed variance ($\\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\\ $0.026$); on RE, only VC consistently outperforms LP (preliminary).\nWhen model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\\ref{tab:wnut}).\n\n\\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}\n\\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.\nConsensus-proximity selection (\\S\\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\\ref{tab:selection}).\n\\textit{Layer 2 (score compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 13--18~pp oracle headroom.\nLP scores are severely compressed: 60\\% of instances have a within-sample range below 0.05, and 75\\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\\Delta|{<}0.026$; Appendix~\\ref{app:logprob_ties}).\nIn the 40\\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \\textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\\rho$: 0.08$\\to$0.39).\nThis diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression is the primary mechanistic bottleneck.\nA controlled ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that this compression is intrinsic to the model and task, not an artifact of constrained decoding.\nDiversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.\n\n\\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}\nOur selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \\cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\\hat{y} = \\arg\\max_{y_i} \\sum_{j \\neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.\nDespite MBR's success in machine translation \\cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \\cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.\n\\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.\n\n\\paragraph{Score compression under free-form decoding.}\\label{sec:ablation}\nA natural hypothesis is that LP compression is an artifact of constrained decoding's restricted token space.\nWe test this via controlled ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, single dataset): generating free-form (unconstrained) outputs on the same instances with post-hoc JSON parsing (parse rate 99.95\\%, 4406/4408; Table~\\ref{tab:freeform_ablation}).\nFor NER, LP variance is essentially unchanged (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\\times}$, tied fraction 59.7\\%$\\to$57.7\\%) and selection gains remain negligible ($+0.18$~pp free-form vs.\\ $+0.59$~pp constrained), establishing that NER LP compression persists independent of decoding regime in our setting.\nHowever, the ablation reveals a task-dependent interaction: RE LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single seed), suggesting that constrained decoding may be a contributing factor for RE even though it is not for NER.\nThe NER/RE divergence indicates that the relationship between decoding regime and selection is task-specific rather than universal.\nNotably, the fine-tuned model achieved 99.95\\% parse rate without grammar constraints, suggesting that constrained decoding's format-compliance role may be redundant for sufficiently fine-tuned models.\n\n\\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}\nThe free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.\nOn RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).\nThe win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).\nThis interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.\nThis ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); multi-seed replication is left for future work.\nSecond, the non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472, indicating that 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, yielding a $3{\\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.\nDespite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible---score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.\nFree-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\\rho$: 0.379$\\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.\n\n\\paragraph{Methodological implications.}\nThe decoupling of quality estimation ($\\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.\nEffective selection likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \\cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\\ref{app:additional}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.\nCross-dataset evaluation confirms that structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (VC $\\rho{=}0.469$ OOD vs.\\ $0.386$ in-domain); the reverse direction fails due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure (Appendix~\\ref{app:ood}).\nOur findings are established under constrained decoding at 8B scale; a single-dataset NER ablation suggests LP compression persists without constrained decoding, but RE shows task-dependent interaction with decoding regime.\nWhether these patterns generalize across datasets, model scales, and decoding strategies warrants further investigation.\n",

    "originalFile": "\\section{Discussion}\\label{sec:discussion}\n\n\\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}\nFor per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\\rho{=}0.38$), though EM leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).\nSignal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.\nAt higher sample sizes ($N{=}16$), SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\\Delta{=}0.002$) with lower cross-seed variance ($\\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\\ $0.026$); on RE, only VC consistently outperforms LP (preliminary).\nWhen model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\\ref{tab:wnut}).\n\n\\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}\n\\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.\nConsensus-proximity selection (\\S\\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\\ref{tab:selection}).\n\\textit{Layer 2 (score compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 13--18~pp oracle headroom.\nLP scores are severely compressed: the median within-instance LP range is only 0.041 nats, below the $\\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold at which 60\\% of instances are effectively tied, and 75\\% of pairwise comparisons fall within $|\\Delta|{<}0.026$ (Appendix~\\ref{app:logprob_ties}).\nIn the 40\\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \\textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\\rho$: 0.08$\\to$0.39).\nThis diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression is the primary mechanistic bottleneck.\nA controlled ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that this compression is intrinsic to the model and task, not an artifact of constrained decoding.\nDiversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.\n\n\\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}\nOur selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \\cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\\hat{y} = \\arg\\max_{y_i} \\sum_{j \\neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.\nDespite MBR's success in machine translation \\cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \\cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.\n\\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.\n\n\\paragraph{Score compression under free-form decoding.}\\label{sec:ablation}\nA natural hypothesis is that LP compression is an artifact of constrained decoding's restricted token space.\nWe test this via controlled ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, single dataset): generating free-form (unconstrained) outputs on the same instances with post-hoc JSON parsing (parse rate 99.95\\%, 4406/4408; Table~\\ref{tab:freeform_ablation}).\nFor NER, LP variance is essentially unchanged (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\\times}$, tied fraction 59.7\\%$\\to$57.7\\%) and selection gains remain negligible ($+0.18$~pp free-form vs.\\ $+0.59$~pp constrained), establishing that NER LP compression persists independent of decoding regime in our setting.\nHowever, the ablation reveals a task-dependent interaction: RE LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single seed), suggesting that constrained decoding may be a contributing factor for RE even though it is not for NER.\nThe NER/RE divergence indicates that the relationship between decoding regime and selection is task-specific rather than universal.\nNotably, the fine-tuned model achieved 99.95\\% parse rate without grammar constraints, suggesting that constrained decoding's format-compliance role may be redundant for sufficiently fine-tuned models.\n\n\\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}\nThe free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.\nOn RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).\nThe win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).\nThis interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.\nThis ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); multi-seed replication is left for future work.\nSecond, the non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472, indicating that 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, yielding a $3{\\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.\nDespite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible---score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.\nFree-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\\rho$: 0.379$\\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.\n\n\\paragraph{Methodological implications.}\nThe decoupling of quality estimation ($\\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.\nEffective selection likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \\cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\\ref{app:additional}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.\nCross-dataset evaluation confirms that structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (VC $\\rho{=}0.469$ OOD vs.\\ $0.386$ in-domain); the reverse direction fails due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure (Appendix~\\ref{app:ood}).\nOur findings are established under constrained decoding at 8B scale; a single-dataset NER ablation suggests LP compression persists without constrained decoding, but RE shows task-dependent interaction with decoding regime.\nWhether these patterns generalize across datasets, model scales, and decoding strategies warrants further investigation.\n",

当前 abstract 第 2 句 "uncover a correlation-selection gap" 和第 3 句 "instance-level by construction" 矛盾——先说"发现"再说"定义上如此"。

**修改方案**：
- Sentence 2：只写 LP compression + MBR failure 的实证发现
- Sentence 3：用从句铺垫 definitional 前提，如 "Given that four of five signals are instance-level by construction, the empirical question is whether... Neither succeeds: ..."
- 确保 "discover" vs "definitional" 的叙事逻辑通顺

## 2. C4 Scope Language 降级

全文搜索 "fundamental"/"intrinsic" 等过强用词：
- 替换为 "observed in our NER/RE setting at 8B scale"
- 但在 Discussion 中可保留有限 universality 表述："intrinsic to the model-task interaction"（有 ablation 证据支撑：temperature/prompt/N 均无法消除 gap）

## 3. Q3 RE Flip 处理

RE LP 翻转 (-0.68→+1.69pp) 在 bootstrap 95% CI [-3.0, +4.2]pp 内，single seed。
- 主文承认翻转存在
- 报告 CI 说明不显著
- 不升级为 claim
- Discussion 加一句："RE 在 free-form 下的行为值得进一步研究（single-seed limitation）"

## 4. Appendix 模型名修复（Critical）

Appendix 表格中 "Qwen 2.5-7B" 需全部替换为 "Qwen3-8B"。全文搜索确保无遗漏。

## 5. W6 Limitations 段落

T=0.7 LP 数据不存在，不补跑。在 Limitations 中添加：当前 LP 分析仅覆盖 T=1.0，T=0.7 下的 LP compression 行为有待验证。同时强调 free-form ablation（std ratio 0.97）作为 temperature-robustness 的更强证据。

## 6. C5 标题

维持不变，不改。

1	\begin{abstract}
2	Test-time scaling through repeated sampling promises quality gains for LLM-based information extraction (IE), but whether confidence signals can identify the best output among multiple candidates remains untested for structured tasks.
3	We evaluate five confidence signals on three NER benchmarks and one RE benchmark with two 8B-parameter model families.
4	All signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38, AUROC up to 0.75) yet none significantly improves sample selection despite 13--18~pp oracle headroom---a \textit{correlation-selection gap}.
5	For four of five signals, selection failure follows from their definition as instance-level scores; the empirical question is whether per-sample log-probability or consensus-proximity selection (MBR decoding) can bridge the gap.
6	Neither succeeds: log-probability scores are compressed into effective ties within instances, and MBR utility correlates with quality across instances but not within them.
7	A controlled ablation on NER confirms that LP compression persists without constrained decoding; on RE, LP selection reverses direction, suggesting task-dependent interaction with decoding regime.
8	These findings, consistent across two model families at 8B scale, indicate that closing the gap likely requires per-sample scoring beyond unsupervised signals.
9	\end{abstract}
10	
```

    "originalFile": "Our evaluation covers three datasets but only one RE benchmark (SciERC), where 40\\% of instances receive zero F1, compressing the discriminable range and limiting signal differentiation for relation extraction.\nRE selection failure persists even when restricting to non-zero F1 instances (Appendix~\\ref{app:re_conditional_selection}), ruling out floor effects as the sole explanation, but generalization to other RE benchmarks remains unvalidated.\nWNUT-17 confirms the capability boundary of our approach, but our positive results on formal-domain text (CoNLL, SciERC) have not been validated on informal or noisy text where models achieve non-trivial performance.\n\nWe evaluate two model families (Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B), both at 8B parameters.\nA 3-seed robustness analysis confirms that signal rankings are stable across seeds ($\\sigma{\\leq}0.026$; Table~\\ref{tab:multiseed}), but whether our findings---particularly the correlation-selection gap and the difficulty-dependent signal ordering---hold for larger models (70B+) or closed-source APIs remains untested.\nLarger models may produce higher-quality and more diverse samples, potentially altering the signal landscape.\n\nOur analysis of selection potential uses only unsupervised signals.\nWe do not train a dedicated verifier or reward model, leaving unknown how much of the oracle headroom a supervised approach could recover.\n\nWe evaluate at $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$.\nThe behavior of confidence signals at larger sample sizes (e.g., $N{=}64$ or $N{=}128$) is unknown, and $N$-scaling gains are setting-dependent: SJ improves by $+0.047$ on Qwen SciERC NER but only $+0.016$ on LLaMA SciERC NER when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$.\n\nOn CoNLL with LLaMA, the SJ--FK gap is only 0.003 ($\\rho{=}0.431$ vs.\\ $0.428$), so the structural advantage over surface signals may not generalize to all simple-schema datasets.\nOur free-form ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that LP score compression persists without constrained decoding, but was conducted on a single dataset (SciERC) with one model (Qwen3-8B); whether the intrinsic compression finding generalizes to other datasets, model families, or model scales remains untested.\n\nQwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with \\texttt{enable\\_thinking} active, injecting empty \\texttt{&lt;think>&lt;/think>} blocks (4--5 tokens, no reasoning chain) before each response; CoNLL and WNUT checkpoints disabled this feature.\nAt inference time, constrained decoding suppresses thinking tokens in all configurations, so they do not appear in generated samples.\nThe empty blocks may weakly affect first-token probability distributions during training, potentially shifting LP score calibration on SciERC; however, since LP selection fails across all datasets including CoNLL and WNUT-17 (which lack this confound), the thinking token inconsistency is unlikely to explain the correlation-selection gap.\nThe absence of any reasoning content further limits the representational impact.\n\nFinally, log-probability was excluded from the temperature comparison ($T{=}0.7$ vs.\\ $T{=}1.0$) due to missing $T{=}0.7$ LP data, leaving its temperature sensitivity uncharacterized.\n",

```text
24	\paragraph{Score compression under free-form decoding.}\label{sec:ablation}
25	A natural hypothesis is that LP compression is an artifact of constrained decoding's restricted token space.
26	We test this via controlled ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, single dataset): generating free-form (unconstrained) outputs on the same instances with post-hoc JSON parsing (parse rate 99.95\%, 4406/4408; Table~\ref{tab:freeform_ablation}).
27	For NER, LP variance is essentially unchanged (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\times}$, tied fraction 59.7\%$\to$57.7\%) and selection gains remain negligible ($+0.18$~pp free-form vs.\ $+0.59$~pp constrained), establishing that NER LP compression persists independent of decoding regime in our setting.
28	However, the ablation reveals a task-dependent interaction: RE LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single seed), suggesting that constrained decoding may be a contributing factor for RE even though it is not for NER.
29	The NER/RE divergence indicates that the relationship between decoding regime and selection is task-specific rather than universal.
30	Notably, the fine-tuned model achieved 99.95\% parse rate without grammar constraints, suggesting that constrained decoding's format-compliance role may be redundant for sufficiently fine-tuned models.
31	
32	\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
33	The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
34	On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
35	The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
36	This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
37	This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); multi-seed replication is left for future work.
38	Second, the non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472, indicating that 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, yielding a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
39	Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible---score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
40	Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.
41	
42	\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
43	The decoupling of quality estimation ($\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.
```

    "originalFile": "\\section{Discussion}\\label{sec:discussion}\n\n\\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}\nFor per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\\rho{=}0.38$), though EM leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).\nSignal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.\nAt higher sample sizes ($N{=}16$), SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\\Delta{=}0.002$) with lower cross-seed variance ($\\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\\ $0.026$); on RE, only VC consistently outperforms LP (preliminary).\nWhen model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\\ref{tab:wnut}).\n\n\\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}\n\\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.\nConsensus-proximity selection (\\S\\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\\ref{tab:selection}).\n\\textit{Layer 2 (score compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 13--18~pp oracle headroom.\nLP scores are severely compressed: the median within-instance LP range is only 0.041 nats, below the $\\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold at which 60\\% of instances are effectively tied, and 75\\% of pairwise comparisons fall within $|\\Delta|{<}0.026$ (Appendix~\\ref{app:logprob_ties}).\nIn the 40\\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \\textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\\rho$: 0.08$\\to$0.39).\nThis diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression is the primary mechanistic bottleneck.\nA controlled NER ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that LP compression persists without constrained decoding; on RE, the interaction is task-dependent.\nDiversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.\n\n\\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}\nOur selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \\cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\\hat{y} = \\arg\\max_{y_i} \\sum_{j \\neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.\nDespite MBR's success in machine translation \\cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \\cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.\n\\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.\n\n\\paragraph{Score compression under free-form decoding.}\\label{sec:ablation}\nA natural hypothesis is that LP compression is an artifact of constrained decoding's restricted token space.\nWe test this via controlled ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, single dataset): generating free-form (unconstrained) outputs on the same instances with post-hoc JSON parsing (parse rate 99.95\\%, 4406/4408;     "originalFile": "\\section{Discussion}\\label{sec:discussion}\n\n\\paragraph{Practical recommendations.}\nFor per-instance quality ranking, VC provides the strongest rank correlation ($\\rho{=}0.38$), though EM leads binary discrimination (AUROC${=}0.749$); under conditional filtering, EM leads on both NER and RE ($\\rho{=}0.360$, $0.417$; RE: preliminary, single benchmark).\nSignal rankings depend on task difficulty---EM dominates easy tasks (CoNLL), VC and SJ dominate hard tasks (SciERC)---directionally consistent across two model families at 8B scale, though with model-dependent magnitude.\nAt higher sample sizes ($N{=}16$), SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\\Delta{=}0.002$) with lower cross-seed variance ($\\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\\ $0.026$); on RE, only VC consistently outperforms LP (preliminary).\nWhen model capability is insufficient (WNUT-17), all signals converge toward non-significant conditional correlations (Table~\\ref{tab:wnut}).\n\n\\paragraph{Why the gap exists: two layers.}\n\\textit{Layer 1 (definitional):} Four of five signals are instance-level aggregates that assign a single score per input; they cannot rank candidates by construction.\nConsensus-proximity selection (\\S\\ref{sec:evaluation}) does not recover per-sample discrimination (Table~\\ref{tab:selection}).\n\\textit{Layer 2 (score compression):} Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, also fails to exploit the 13--18~pp oracle headroom.\nLP scores are severely compressed: the median within-instance LP range is only 0.041 nats, below the $\\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold at which 60\\% of instances are effectively tied, and 75\\% of pairwise comparisons fall within $|\\Delta|{<}0.026$ (Appendix~\\ref{app:logprob_ties}).\nIn the 40\\% of instances where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP \\textit{significantly} outperforms greedy ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.01$; within-instance $\\rho$: 0.08$\\to$0.39).\nThis diagnostic confirms that LP carries useful per-sample quality information; score compression is the primary mechanistic bottleneck.\nA controlled NER ablation (\\S\\ref{sec:ablation}) confirms that LP compression persists without constrained decoding; on RE, the interaction is task-dependent.\nDiversity-stratified analysis confirms the gap persists even among high-diversity instances (Appendix~\\ref{app:diversity}); RE miscalibration (ECE 0.109--0.339, preliminary; Appendix~\\ref{app:calibration}) may compound this.\n\n\\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}\nOur selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \\cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\\hat{y} = \\arg\\max_{y_i} \\sum_{j \\neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.\nDespite MBR's success in machine translation \\cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \\cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here because the utility functions correlate with F1 at the instance level but not within a single instance---the mathematical essence of the correlation-selection gap.\n\\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs---consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.\n\n\\paragraph{Score compression under free-form decoding.}\\label{sec:ablation}\nA natural hypothesis is that LP compression is an artifact of constrained decoding's restricted token space.\nWe test this via controlled ablation on SciERC (Qwen3-8B, single dataset): generating free-form (unconstrained) outputs on the same instances with post-hoc JSON parsing (parse rate 99.95\\%, 4406/4408; Table~\\ref{tab:freeform_ablation}).\nFor NER, LP variance is essentially unchanged (within-instance std ratio $0.97{\\times}$, tied fraction 59.7\\%$\\to$57.7\\%) and selection gains remain negligible ($+0.18$~pp free-form vs.\\ $+0.59$~pp constrained), establishing that NER LP compression persists independent of decoding regime in our setting.\nHowever, the ablation reveals a task-dependent interaction: RE LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single seed).\nThis reversal falls within the NER bootstrap 95\\% CI [$-3.0$, $+4.2$]~pp and is based on a single seed, so we do not treat it as a confirmed finding; it suggests that constrained decoding may interact differently with RE but requires multi-seed replication.\nThe NER/RE divergence indicates that the relationship between decoding regime and selection is task-specific in our setting.\nNotably, the fine-tuned model achieved 99.95\\% parse rate without grammar constraints, suggesting that constrained decoding's format-compliance role may be redundant for sufficiently fine-tuned models.\n\n\\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}\nThe free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.\nOn RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).\nThe win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).\nThis interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.\nThis ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); multi-seed replication is left for future work.\nSecond, the non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472, indicating that 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, yielding a $3{\\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.\nDespite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible---score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.\nFree-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\\rho$: 0.379$\\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.\n\n\\paragraph{Methodological implications.}\nThe decoupling of quality estimation ($\\rho$), binary discrimination (AUROC), and sample selection (best-of-$N$ F1) means evaluating on a single metric risks selecting the wrong signal for the intended use case.\nEffective selection likely requires per-sample signals such as trained verifiers \\cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}; $N$-scaling analysis (Appendix~\\ref{app:additional}) shows $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit.\nCross-dataset evaluation confirms that structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (VC $\\rho{=}0.469$ OOD vs.\\ $0.386$ in-domain); the reverse direction fails due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure (Appendix~\\ref{app:ood}).\nOur findings are established under constrained decoding at 8B scale; a single-dataset NER ablation suggests LP compression persists without constrained decoding, but RE shows task-dependent interaction with decoding regime.\nWhether these patterns generalize across datasets, model scales, and decoding strategies warrants further investigation.\n",
